overview.text: Lithium (Li) is chemical element 3, a group 1 alkali metal and the lightest metal. At room temperature it is a soft, silvery solid with exceptionally low density, but it reacts vigorously with water; it occurs naturally in minerals and brines rather than as pure metal. Its standout modern role is in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in portable electronics and electric vehicles: lithium-containing electrolytes and compounds are part of cells that also contain other electrode materials. Lithium compounds are also used in specialty glass and ceramics, while lithium alloys can make some metals stronger and lighter. These applications make this lightweight element important to electronics and transport.

key_facts.text: Symbol Li; atomic number 3; located in group 1 of the periodic table.
A soft, silvery solid at room temperature, lithium is the least dense of the metals and reacts vigorously with water.
Lithium is found in nature in minerals and brines, not as pure metal.
Lithium-ion batteries are used in electronics and vehicles; their cells include lithium-containing electrolytes and other electrode materials.
Lithium compounds are used in glass and ceramics, and lithium alloys can help make metals stronger and lighter.
